context: modular plant · containers set on pads in weeks; grid connection, fire approval and grid-code tests govern

brief.intro: New to this project type? A battery energy storage plant is rows of factory-built containers full of lithium battery racks, each with its own cooling and fire system, connected through power-conversion units (inverters) and transformers to a substation and the grid. Almost nothing is built on site: the civil work is pads, roads, cable trenches and a fence, and the containers are lifted into place in days. That is what misleads newcomers — the site work is short, but the project is long. The grid connection agreement and the substation, the delivery of containers and transformers, the fire authority's approval of the layout, and above all the testing — commissioning every container, then proving to the grid operator that the plant responds as the grid code requires — decide the completion date.

glossary.plain: power conversion system — the inverter that changes battery DC into grid AC and back.
battery management system — monitors every cell and protects the battery.
the control system that decides when the plant charges and discharges.
power (how fast it can charge or discharge) and energy (how long it can do so).
a battery cell overheating uncontrollably — the fire risk that the layout and protection are designed around.
the technical rules a plant must meet to be connected — response, ride-through, reactive power.
a full charge-discharge test proving the contracted energy.
adding batteries later to make up for ageing; space is often left for it.

must_get_right: The grid connection (agreement, substation, main transformer, energisation date) is usually the critical path — start it first and show it as its own chain.
Containers and transformers are the long-lead items; site works are short and should be timed to finish just before they arrive, not months earlier.
Settle the fire strategy with the authority before the layout is frozen — spacing between containers decides how much fits on the site.
Leave real time for commissioning and grid-code compliance tests; the grid operator witnesses them and they can take weeks after energisation.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Activities are organised by block (a group of containers with its PCS and transformer) and by the substation, so each block can be commissioned and counted as available capacity.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Standard site calendar. Energisation and grid-code tests are dated activities agreed with the grid operator; some tests need particular grid conditions.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: Two chains meet at energisation: (1) grid agreement → substation → main transformer → pre-energisation tests; (2) pads → containers and PCS → cabling → cold commissioning. Then energisation → hot commissioning by block → capacity test → grid-code tests → commercial operation. The critical path normally runs through the grid connection or the main transformer.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: The connection agreement is signed on the assumed date; the grid operator builds or releases its side of the connection on time; containers ship fully tested; the fire authority accepts the layout as designed.

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Heavy lifts need hardstanding and crane access to every pad. Batteries are dangerous goods in transport and storage; they should not sit on site for long before installation and must be kept within a charge and temperature range.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Main risks: late grid connection or transformer, container delivery, fire-authority comments changing spacing, communication problems between BMS, PCS and EMS, and failed compliance tests. Contingency is held before the commercial operation date.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3 by block and substation; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the installation and commissioning teams — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
